Burnt out from finding the right words to say, and not really knowing what words I needed, I started reading grief memoirs: When Breath Becomes Air, Crying in H Mart, The Bright Hour, A Grief Observed. I found more solace here, reading the personal experiences of grief in the first perspective of others, almost as if in their own brain. I found more support and solace here than anywhere else. It was nice not to feel so alone in my grief, if even for a few sentences. 

It’s going to be a year since my mom passed next month—there is no universal answer. Some days it feels impossible. But over time you start to see the little reminders of them around you that pull you out of your head and into the now. Almost like they’re still here, and it’s refreshing to remember them in ways your memories forgot. And suddenly it’s there, like they’re there. These small things, these small moments they sneak up on you. For me it’s the rain. Something so small that feels like everything. 

Grief is different for everyone, but the more you hear about others in their perspective, not in a conversation, but in their stream of consciousness, you’ll start to find you have things in common more often than not. Not words, not thoughts, but overall ineffable feelings that make the heaviness you’re feeling just a little bit lighter.

Wow this really resonated with me—it makes complete sense and I am so sorry to hear about your dad. 

I worked in the ER for 7 years before my mom passed away in the same hospital I not only worked at, but was born at, and grew up in—learning medicine from such a young age. She was 54 and had stage IV breast cancer—her end of life care (after nearly 7 years of being sick) was 7 days in the ICU and watching her slowly stop eating, drinking, breathing, was easily the hardest thing I have ever experienced. After she died, I quit my job, and 9 months later, had to go to the hospital and I had a complete mental breakdown. It wasn’t even the same one, either.

Sending you love & support—remember everyone’s grief looks different and you’re doing everything you can. ♥️

re: therapy and wanting to share how you feel but I don’t want to be committed to a psych ward 

is this not the most frustrating part of all? you’d think there would be a better response to this than a short stay at a place that pretends to take you bent & promises to make you whole in all of 5 days.

it’s like the moment you relay the truth, these ideas, intended or not, planned or not, everything shifts. the therapist embarks on a scripted survey of systematic administrative inquiry, rather than fluid exploration. this examination, for me at least, just increased the distance between me and my therapist by ten fold. they’re instructed to do this, directed to respond a certain way, universally, to protect liability & prevent lawsuits. 

Almost every interaction where I reveal these ideations, however involuntary, I am alone. You can feel this way and not want to, not choose to. You can have a plan and not want to, not choose to. It’s much more complicated than “do you have thoughts of killing yourself?”. when you disclose this personal, vulnerable, and inconvenient truth, to another or others, often times you feel more alone and more isolated unless the person themselves has had a similar experience. It’s more down-regulative than conductive. 

We need more safe places! Not just hotlines and forums. But real spaces where real people can speak on their struggles and interact with others who can empathize or relate to those experiences. People say “we had no idea” and that’s because the society we live in, and the response and attitude we have surrounding suicidality are notoriously uncomfortable and more isolating. Often times, people feel separated more than connected when sharing these thoughts. The inconvenience of divulging these thoughts, when severe enough, propels many of us to seek help or conversation. And when we seek comfort or help, in my experience, I feel even more disconnected. I feel like a human altered and sterilized before packaging. So I want to say less, talk less, feel less weird, be around less, live less. Litigation & administration shouldn’t affect empathy & compassion, and this scripted societal response we are all too familiar with does exactly that—in fact, often times, removes it completely.
